{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=intelligent+judgment+obedience+conflicting+instructions+decision+theory&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Invisible Erosion of Human Capital: The Impact of Emotional Blackmail and Emotional Intelligence on Nurses' Job Satisfaction and Turnover Intention.\", \"abstract\": \"Emotion is a compelling factor in the retention and job satisfaction of professionals, and the impacts of emotional feelings and reactions have become an indispensable issue in the nursing workforce. Drawing on the cognitive theory of emotions, this study bridges the research gap to investigate the relationships among emotional blackmail, emotional intelligence, job satisfaction, and turnover intentions of nurses. A cross-sectional design was used to collect data from a sample of 374 full-time nurses in Northern Taiwan. Hypotheses were tested and analyzed by means of SPSS 22, structural equation modeling (SEM), and PROCESS v3.3. The results revealed the direct relationships between emotional blackmail, job satisfaction, and turnover intentions, and job satisfaction partially mediated the relationship between emotional blackmail and turnover intentions. However, there is no statistical support that emotional intelligence moderates the relationships between emotional blackmail and job satisfaction and turnover intentions. Healthcare organizations must take the initiative and form strategies that will help balance nurses' work stresses. These strategies should aim to reduce unnecessary demands from supervisors, patients, and co-workers, as well as in the socio-emotional domain.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/bs13010037\", \"pmid\": \"36661609\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC9854503\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Unpaywall\", \"url\": \"https://www.mdpi.com/2076-328X/13/1/37/pdf?version=1672466730\"}, {\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3390/bs13010037\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"…

{"url": "https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.findings-acl.67", "scope": "extracted web-page text; may be incomplete", "excerpt": "Nuclear Deployed!: Analyzing Catastrophic Risks in Decision-making of Autonomous LLM Agents - ACL Anthology
Nuclear Deployed!: Analyzing Catastrophic Risks in Decision-making of Autonomous
LLM
Agents
Rongwu Xu
,
Xiaojian Li
,
Shuo Chen
,
Wei Xu
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) are evolving into autonomous decision-makers, raising concerns about catastrophic risks in high-stakes scenarios, particularly in Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear (CBRN) domains. Based on the insight that such risks can originate from trade-offs between the agent’s Helpful, Harmlessness and Honest (HHH) goals, we build a novel three-stage evaluation framework, which is carefully constructed to effectively and naturally expose such risks. We conduct 14,400 agentic simulations across 12 advanced LLMs, with extensive experiments and analysis. Results reveal that LLM agents can autonomously engage in catastrophic behaviors and deception, without being deliberately induced. Furthermore, stronger reasoning abilities often increase, rather than mitigate, these risks. We also show that these agents can violate instructions and superior commands. On the whole, we empirically prove the existence of catastrophic risks in autonomous LLM agents.

{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=artificial+agency+moral+responsibility+accountability+decision+consequences+attribution&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7483422\", \"title\": [\"Self-Good Desire and the Moral Agency of Artificial Intelligence :A Criterion of Life Integrity for Responsibility Attribution\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The increasing autonomy of artificial intelligence has intensified the \\\"responsibility gap\\\" and the debate over AI moral agency. Existing accounts commonly appeal to rational capacity, sentience, or functional performance, but these criteria do not fully explain either the motivational basis for taking norms as reasons or the conditions under which a subject can bear ultimate moral responsibility. Drawing on the framework developed in On Self-Good Desire, this paper argues that \\\"self-good desire\\\" (sishan yuqiu) is a motivationally necessary condition of full moral agency. It denotes an intrinsic, selfnurturing motivational structure through which a living subject maintains its existence, improves its condition, and pursues its development, unfolding into eleven root desires: self-preservation, self-care, self-enrichment, self-beautification, self-joy, self-compassion, self-reflection, self-confidence, selfstrengthening, self-respect, and freedom. \\\"Life integrity\\\" here does not reduce moral agency to a particular biological substrate; rather, it refers to an integrated organization of self-maintenance, felt value, diachronic identity, and self-concern. Self-good desire is not sufficient for full moral agency, which also requires normative understanding, behavioral control, and responsibility-bearing capacity. On this account, current AI systems can represent norms and simulate forms of moral reasoning, yet there is presently insufficient warrant to attribute to them endogenous needs, first-person experience, enduring self-concern, or genuinely self-generated stakes. They therefore should not be treated as full moral agents. When AI systems cause harm, ultimate moral responsibility should ordinarily remain with human and institutional actors and be allocated by reference to control, causal contribution, benefit, foreseeability, and duties of care.
